title: Austin Instrument, Inc. v. Loral Corporation
summary: Loral established economic duress when an indispensable supplier withheld precision gears to extract price increases that Loral could not practicably resist.
notes:
29 N.Y.2d 124 (1971), decided July 6, 1971 by a 4-3 vote: Chief Judge Fuld wrote for the majority (Burke, Scileppi and Gibson concurring), and Judge Bergan's dissent was joined by Judges Breitel and Jasen.

The majority's test: economic duress exists where one party is forced to agree to a modification by a wrongful threat precluding the exercise of free will, such as a threat to withhold needed goods when the victim cannot obtain them from another source and an ordinary breach-of-contract action would be inadequate.

sections.Parties: Austin manufactured precision gears for Loral, a Navy radar contractor. Austin sought unpaid sums under a second subcontract; Loral sought return of the increases paid under the first subcontract.
sections.Material Facts:
Loral’s first Navy contract, worth $6 million, required scheduled radar deliveries and included provisions for late-delivery damages and cancellation on default. Austin received a subcontract for 23 of approximately 40 gear components. When Loral later obtained a second Navy contract, Austin demanded all 40 components rather than only the items on which it was low bidder. It also demanded increased prices under the existing subcontract, both for parts already delivered and for future deliveries, and stopped supplying parts.

Loral contacted all ten manufacturers on its approved list. None could commence deliveries soon enough to protect the September and October radar deadlines; even the best response promised only a start in October. Precision standards made unfamiliar vendors an inadequate immediate substitute. Loral agreed in a protest letter explaining the absence of alternatives. It ultimately met the Navy deadlines with Austin’s resumed deliveries. Three days after Austin’s final delivery under the second subcontract, Loral demanded a refund of the increases.
sections.Procedural History: The parties’ actions were consolidated. After trial, Austin received the amount due on the second subcontract, and Loral’s claim was dismissed. A divided Appellate Division affirmed. The New York Court of Appeals modified the order, reversing dismissal of Loral’s claim and remanding for calculation of its damages. Loral did not challenge the second subcontract in this action.
sections.Issue: Did the supply stoppage and associated demands make the price increases voidable for economic duress, and did Loral lose its remedy by waiting until deliveries ended?
sections.Holding: The majority found economic duress as a matter of law on the accepted facts. Loral’s delay was reasonable while further supply pressure remained possible.
sections.Reasoning:
A threat to breach a supply contract alone does not establish economic duress. The threatened party must lack an adequate alternative source of the needed goods, and ordinary breach damages must be insufficient. Here a later damages award could not itself obtain the precision components needed to meet the Navy schedule. Loral faced contractual penalties, possible default, and damage to its important government business. Those concerns were concrete consequences of the threatened stoppage.

The majority considered Loral’s supplier search adequate. It was not required to gamble on unapproved manufacturers or obtain an uncertain extension from the Navy. The alternatives could not promise timely full supply. Loral also had reason to postpone disaffirmance: Austin had demonstrated a willingness to stop deliveries and could have repeated the pressure while the second order remained incomplete. A demand three days after final delivery was consequently timely.

The case is a useful example of common-law defenses supplementing a goods transaction. The editors direct the reader to UCC § 1-103(b), because Article 2 does not itself set out the rules of duress.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: It explains what must be shown in addition to a threat of breach: practical inability to replace the promised performance and an inadequate damages remedy.

topics.duress: Supply alternatives, timing, and the inadequacy of damages determine whether consent to higher prices was coerced.
topics.modification: The disputed increases changed the first subcontract.
topics.assent: Agreement to a change can be voidable because of the circumstances that induced it.
topics.governing-law: Common-law duress supplements the Article 2 sale of goods.
topics.rescission: Economic duress renders the coerced price increase voidable, and Loral's remedy was to avoid the modification and recover the excess paid.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Bergan’s dissent treated the dispute as factual. It emphasized the findings affirmed below, Austin’s account of a requested vacation shutdown and earlier dissatisfaction, and the possibility of additional suppliers beyond Loral’s approved list. The dissent would not replace those findings with the majority’s conclusion as a matter of law.
